column4: The Rabb's command joins exclusive worship to ihsan toward parents, putting family care inside the Lord's ordering of a home.
The child answers parental raising with mercy: “رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا” explicitly joins Rabb, raḥma, and being raised while small.
Mothers nurse for two complete years, while the father supplies food and clothing; it gives the section's house, duration, nourishment, and completion concrete legal form.
Mary is accepted, made to grow a good growth, and placed in Zakariyya's care; this is Qur'anic tarbiya as gradual growth under a guardian.
God fashions people “فِي الْأَرْحَامِ” as He wills, making the womb the place of divine formation described by the section.
“Creation after creation” in mothers' wombs makes the womb a hidden dwelling of successive formation rather than a single moment.
The drop is put in a secure resting-place, a direct Qur'anic counterpart to the womb as a child's enclosing home.
The passage moves the embryo through distinct states until another creation, directly realizing tarbiya as being brought state by state toward completion.
Human origin from a weak fluid begins the sequence whose protected place and measured term follow in this passage.
The fluid is placed in a “firm resting-place,” a particularly close parallel to the womb as container and house.
Its “known measure” supplies the duration within which the section says mercy and growth work.
God's determining completes the preceding protected-place image: formation has a measure and an active determiner.
It explicitly traces embryonic stages, remaining in wombs for an appointed term, infancy, and maturity; the whole arc is the section's place-and-time growth.
Pregnancy and birth come with hardship, followed by weaning and full strength; it includes the mother's cost that the she-camel dictionary sense keeps visible.
The mother carries weakness upon weakness and weans over two years, grounding filial gratitude in bodily, gradual maternal care.
It orders housing and provision for a pregnant mother, payment for nursing, and another nurse if needed: care can be shared without abandoning the child.
Humans emerge from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts, joining birth to the beginning of learning.
God knows what every womb carries and its decrease and increase, with everything measured; hidden gestation is both known and ordered.
No female conceives or gives birth outside God's knowledge, explicitly placing pregnancy and delivery under divine care.
The ayah runs from reproductive origin through childhood and full strength to old age, an extended Qur'anic sequence of human growth.
The emitted drop recalls the first, dependent state before the later making and proportioning in the next ayat.
The drop becomes a clinging form, preserving the section's attention to distinct formative stages.
God makes and proportionates, then differentiates male and female; formation is purposeful rather than merely biological.
A wife carries a light burden which becomes heavy, making pregnancy itself a scene of shared human dependence and appeal to God.
The wife of ʿImran dedicates what is in her womb before birth, treating the unborn child as already held in a divine and familial trust.
At Mary's birth her mother names her and seeks protection for her and her descendants, extending maternal care into prayerful safeguarding.
Mary conceives and withdraws with the child to a distant place, staging pregnancy as a sheltered but exposed maternal passage.
Labor pains drive Mary to the palm trunk, a direct birth scene that gives bodily cost to the commentary's maternal image.
At childbirth she is told not to grieve and is provided a stream; divine mercy appears as immediate care for a vulnerable mother.
Fresh dates are provided through the palm, turning provision into bodily support during the birth scene.
“Eat, drink, and be comforted” completes the care of Mary after delivery rather than leaving mercy as an abstraction.
Moses' mother is commanded to nurse him, then entrust him amid danger; it makes maternal feeding and fear part of the child's first care.
Pharaoh's wife proposes that the found child may be a comfort or be taken as a son, opening the question of a home beyond biological parentage.
The mother's heart becomes empty after separation, showing the wound left when the child leaves the maternal enclosure.
Moses refuses other nurses, and his sister offers a household that will take charge of him; nursing, foster care, and a house meet in one ayah.
Moses is returned to his mother so that her eye may be comforted and she not grieve; care restores the broken mother-child bond.
On reaching full strength and maturity Moses receives judgment and knowledge, giving an end point to the childhood-care sequence.
God directs Moses' passage from mother to river to Pharaoh's house so that he may be brought up under God's eye; the true rearer exceeds the visible household.
The sister's intervention returns Moses to his mother for her comfort; this ayah supplies the reunion and maternal relief following 20:39.
Pharaoh says “نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا”; against the prior maternal nursing and divine watchfulness, his claim to have raised Moses is deliberately incomplete.
“رَبَائِبُكُمُ ... فِي حُجُورِكُمْ” names stepdaughters in one's care, directly matching the section's non-birth parent who assumes upbringing.
Property is called a means of qiyām and guardians must provide food, clothing, and kind speech to dependents; it is the household-support sense named for qiwām.
Guardians test orphans until marriageable age and sound judgment before returning their property, making care answerable to a child's gradual maturity.
The wall preserves treasure for two orphan boys until they reach maturity, explicitly calling this delayed protection a mercy from their Lord.
“Improvement for them is best” makes orphan care an active good, and calling them brothers prevents guardianship from becoming exploitation.
It warns people to fear leaving weak offspring behind; the imagined vulnerable children make responsible speech and provision a present duty.
The command to give orphans their property and not consume it with one's own makes material integrity part of care for the weak.
God finds the addressee an orphan and gives shelter, a compact image of divine rearing before the later command concerning orphans.
Finding the addressee in need and enriching him pairs shelter with the household provision developed in the section.
The one who was sheltered as an orphan must not oppress an orphan; received care becomes care for the vulnerable.
The brothers promise both “we will provision our family” and “guard our brother”; its paired acts closely realize the source's secondary senses of household provision and protective care.
The term قَوَّامُونَ is joined to spending from wealth and guarding the unseen, supplying the house-sustaining responsibility developed from the section's qiwām sense.
“Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire” turns guarding the household into a responsibility that includes its ultimate safety.
Children who have not reached puberty learn three household privacy times; the home protects them while teaching boundaries appropriate to their stage.
When children reach puberty they seek permission like adults, marking a concrete transition from one state of household formation to another.
Luqman's address “my son” begins parental teaching with a specific moral boundary against associating partners with God.
Even where parents press toward wrong, the child must accompany them with kindness in this world; filial mercy has a moral boundary without becoming abandonment.
Luqman teaches his son through the mustard-seed image, an example of giving moral knowledge in a small, graspable form.
The father gives his son a sequence of practices—prayer, right action, resistance to wrong, patience—showing formation through teachable acts.
The instruction against contempt and arrogant walking makes character formation part of parental teaching.
Moderating one's walk and voice continues the father's detailed, gradual education of his child.
“رَبَّانِيِّينَ” is tied to teaching and studying the Book, explicitly extending Rabb-root nurture into the work of a teacher.
The rabbāniyyūn are entrusted to guard the Book and bear witness to it; the named derivative joins learning with custodial responsibility.
“الرَّحْمَٰنُ” names the merciful source of the teaching and human-creation sequence in 55:2–4; its own contribution is the teacher's merciful identity.
The Merciful teaches the Qur'an, making instruction itself an act of raḥma rather than a detached transfer of information.
Human creation follows the teaching of the Qur'an, keeping formation and instruction together in the section's order.
Teaching human beings clear expression brings the growing creature into communicative maturity.
The first command to read is in the name of the creating Rabb, joining lordship, creation, and instruction.
Humanity is created from a clinging form; learning is announced beside an early formative state.
The repeated command to read calls the teacher “your Rabb, the Most Generous,” giving generosity to the formative Lord.
Teaching by the pen gives a concrete means by which nurture reaches knowledge.
God teaches the human what he did not know, completing the movement from dependent origin to learned speech.
Moses defines the Rabb as the one who gives every thing its creation and then guides it, a concise cosmic analogue to formation toward its proper end.
Milk from cattle is a pure drink from within their bodies, activating the section's sheep-kept-for-milk sense as nourishment supplied through living creatures.
Cattle provide drink from what is in their bellies and other benefits; it makes animal milk a sign of provision rather than merely an animal fact.
The command to fear God explicitly names “الْأَرْحَامَ”; kinship is held together with the womb word from which the section derives its social sense.
“أُولُو الْأَرْحَامِ” are closer to one another by God's ordinance, giving legal force to the claim that kin share a womb-origin.
The verse again makes those of the arḥām closer in God's Book, distinguishing durable kin obligation from looser social affiliation.
In the annunciation to Sarah, God's mercy and blessing are spoken over “people of the house”; birth promise, house, and raḥma meet explicitly.
Jacob calls God the best guardian and the most merciful, binding protection of a child-like dependent to the divine mercy named by the section.
Jesus' birth is announced as a sign and a mercy from God, linking an extraordinary childbearing scene to mercy made manifest.
Affection and “رَحْمَةً” are placed between spouses; this supplies the relational mercy in which a family home and later child care can exist.
God makes spouses, children, and grandchildren, then provides good things; family generation and household provision are named together.
The prayer for spouses and descendants to be comfort of the eyes makes a flourishing household an object of responsible hope.
The addressee is told to command his family to prayer and persevere, while God—not the caretaker—guarantees provision; spiritual care and sustenance meet.
Abraham and Jacob charge their sons with a durable religious inheritance, a parental form of cultivation beyond bodily upbringing.
Jacob asks his sons what they will worship after him, and their answer displays the fruit of intergenerational teaching at the edge of his death.
Ishmael commands his family to prayer and almsgiving, making care for a household include formed habits of worship and generosity.
When asked what to spend, the ayah names parents, near kin, orphans, and the needy; provision follows the family-and-weakness network of the section.
Righteousness gives cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy, specifying mercy as costly beneficence rather than feeling alone.
Goodness to parents, kin, orphans, and needy neighbors maps a widening household of vulnerable relations that calls for ihsan.
The command for justice, ihsan, and giving to near kin gives Qur'anic form to the section's definition of mercy as tenderness that becomes beneficence.
Those who feed food despite loving it give it to the needy, orphan, and captive; mercy is enacted through nourishment of the vulnerable.
Feeding on a day of hunger makes provision a difficult act, sharpening the section's household-food association.
The hungry person singled out is an orphan of near relationship, where kinship and weakness coincide.
The hard path includes urging one another to patience and “مَرْحَمَة”; compassion is a practiced communal obligation.
Mercy from God makes the Prophet gentle with people; the verse makes raḥma a tenderness that produces a concrete way of treating others.
The Messenger is grieved by believers' hardship and is “رَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ” toward them, giving the mercy-name an attentive, protective stance.
No female conceives or gives birth outside God's knowledge; in an eschatological setting it repeats the hidden maternal scene as a limit on human knowledge.
God knows people best while they are hidden embryos in their mothers' wombs; hidden origin becomes a reason not to declare oneself pure.
Knowledge of what is in wombs belongs to God, preserving the womb as both a real home and a hidden domain beyond human command.
The human is addressed before “your generous Rabb,” so bodily formation is framed as a gift from the nurturing Lord rather than self-production.
God creates, proportions, and balances the human, a compact account of being made fit stage by stage.
God composes the human in whatever form He wills, echoing the form-giving in wombs without repeating its setting.
From a drop God creates and determines the human, linking dependence at origin with measured formation.
God then makes the way easy, extending determination into guided movement through life.
The Creator both makes and proportions; its paired verbs offer a broad formulation of the fitting process behind tarbiya.
Determining and guiding set creation on a directed course, a non-bodily parallel to growth toward its proper limit.
Abraham settles descendants by the Sacred House and asks for provision of fruits; a parent locates children within worship and material sustenance.
Giving the near relative his due, along with the needy and traveler, turns kinship into concrete household-like provision.
The near relative, needy, and traveler receive their due; the ayah makes generous support the better path for those seeking God.
When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend a division, they are to receive provision and kind speech, carrying household resources outward to the weak.
Orphan property may be approached only in the best manner until maturity, matching stewardship that lasts through a child's growth.
The same protection of orphan property “until he reaches maturity” makes legal restraint an expression of long-term care.
God says adopted sons are not one's actual sons; the legal boundary clarifies the section's distinction between biological origin and the person who raises a child.
Calling adopted children by their fathers preserves lineage, while the verse still calls them brothers and clients when parentage is unknown; care survives a boundary of descent.
John receives judgment while still a child, showing divine formation can include early moral and intellectual capacity.
John receives tenderness from God along with purity and piety, a spiritual counterpart to compassion shaping a child.
John is devoted to his parents and not arrogant or disobedient, presenting filial character as an outcome of formed life.
The rabbāniyyūn are blamed for failing to restrain sinful speech and consumption; the named teacher-caretaker role is shown by its neglected duty.
Consuming orphan property unjustly is described as consuming fire; it is the direct opposite of the patient guardianship required for a vulnerable child.
Turning away is described as spreading corruption and severing “أَرْحَامَكُمْ,” reversing the womb-derived bond the section treats as a claim of care.
Following 47:22's severing of kinship ties, this ayah names God's curse and loss of hearing and sight; it supplies the consequence of that rupture.
The command not to kill children from poverty is joined to “We provide for you and them,” reversing fear-driven refusal of the child's provision.
The same prohibition addresses fear of impoverishment and promises provision for children and parents, setting divine sustenance against parental desperation.
Those who kill their children foolishly and forbid God's provision are declared lost; the ayah fuses harm to children with denial of sustenance.
The man given news of a daughter darkens and suppresses grief, a social reversal of receiving a newborn as a mercy and trust.
His deliberation whether to keep the daughter in humiliation or bury her exposes the cruel opposite of sheltering and raising the weak.
The buried girl is summoned to speak, bringing the most vulnerable child into judgment rather than leaving her outside protection.
The question “for what sin was she killed?” condemns the destruction of a daughter where the section sees the child as someone to nurture.
Repulsing the orphan is named as a sign of denying judgment, the contrary of mercy that acts toward the weak.
Alongside 107:2's orphan, failure to urge feeding the poor shows how rejection of the vulnerable includes withholding nourishment.
Failure to honor the orphan is an indictment of a society that treats inherited plenty without the mercy it owes its weak members.
At the Hour, every nursing mother is distracted from the child she nursed and every pregnant woman delivers her burden; the catastrophe reverses ordinary maternal holding and care.
